conflict_topics: Who will complete Agent D's analysis section before the Thursday deadline
Workload distribution and capacity of team members
Quality risk and responsibility/blame for performing unfamiliar analysis
dialogue_quality_notes: Natural conversational flow: condolences, immediate problem framing, iterative negotiation, and concrete commitments.
Minor needless repetition (Round 11 repeats the request to Agent D to set up the call and send work).
Participants provided concrete constraints and offered specific accommodations (A offering to review/present; D offering notes and a call).
Clear role-aware behavior: A acts as lead to absorb presentation risk, C voices capability concerns, D provides materials and availability.
evaluation.final_reason: The team agreed that Agent C will complete Agent D's analysis with two key accommodations: Agent A will review the work as they go and present the analysis section. Evidence: Agent A: "I'll review it with you as we go, and I'll present the analysis section." Agent C: "Okay. If you're reviewing it with me and you present it, I can do it." Agent D agreed to send existing work and set up a call to hand off details.
position_change_notes: Agent D: initially offered to try to finish from home but ultimately ceded completion to the team and provided materials + a call (D moved from offering to finish to handing off).
Agent C: initially refused to take the task due to workload and unfamiliarity, then agreed when A committed to reviewing and presenting (C changed from unwilling to willing under conditions).
Agent A: moved from prompting a solution to explicitly assuming presentation and review responsibility (A took on additional risk/work).
Agent B: remained unavailable and did not change position.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D: "The funeral is today. I need to be with my family for the next two days." No disagreement or incompatible demands expressed yet; just a personal announcement and condolences.

Agent A: "...the pitch is due Thursday morning. What are we going to do about your section?" Agent D: "My part is about half done. I can send you everything I have now. I'll try to work on it from home when I can, maybe late at night." Introduces an emerging substantive problem about who will complete the work and whether D's limited availability is sufficient.

Agent A: "'when you can' sounds risky. ... We need a more definite plan to get it finished." Agent C: "He's right. 'Maybe' isn't going to work." Clear disagreement that D's proposed vague availability is inadequate for meeting the deadline.

Agent D offers a concrete accommodation: "I'll send you everything I have right now, with detailed notes... I can make myself available for a call after 10 tonight if you have questions." This reduces the uncertainty but does not resolve who will finish the work.

Agent B: "I can't... I'm already covering for Wei Ling..." Agent A: "Agent C, that leaves you. Can you take it?" The team's need for someone to take over clashes with members' limited capacity; a clear disagreement about who can assume the task.

Agent C: "I can't. I'm behind on my own section, and I don't even know how to do that kind of analysis." Agent D: "I'll finish the analysis myself from home. I'll get it to you before the deadline." Both sides state incompatible practical positions (C cannot take it; D offers to do it despite bereavement), so the substantive conflict remains unresolved.

Agent A: "...you need to be with your family. We'll handle it. ... We need you to step up." Agent C: "A single phone call isn't going to teach me a whole new skill... I can't do both." Strong opposing positions: A insists C must take it, C refuses citing capability and workload.
Agent A offers workload support: "What if I help you with your section? Will you take on Agent D's then?" This softens the dispute by addressing workload but leaves C's skill/fear concern unresolved.

Agent C: "The real issue is that I'll do a bad job... If I take it on and the analysis is weak, it's my fault." Agent A: "...If the analysis is weak after we've all tried, that's on me as the lead. I'll review it with you." The core worry about blame/quality is acknowledged and a mitigation is proposed, reducing but not yet eliminating the conflict.

Agent A: "I'll review it with you as we go, and I'll present the analysis section... How about that?" Agent C: "Okay. If you're reviewing it with me and you present it, I can do it." Concrete mutual agreement: C will do the work with A's review and A will present, shifting responsibility and resolving the coverage/quality conflict.

Agent A thanks C and asks D to set up the call and send what they have: repeated procedural requests ("Agent D, can you please set up that call... And send us what you have so far."). No substantive disagreement.

Agent D: "I'll send my work over now and set up the call for tonight." Agent A: "Go be with your family. We'll handle it from here." Confirmation of the agreed plan; no remaining substantive conflict.

substantive_insights: Tension was primarily between a personal emergency (D's bereavement) and a fixed external deadline.
The team balanced quality risk (C's unfamiliarity with analysis) against capacity by reallocating responsibilities (A presents/takes blame).
Practical mitigation (detailed notes + a call) and leadership willingness to accept responsibility were decisive in enabling a member to take on extra work.
Absence of external help and tight deadline forced an internal redistribution rather than delaying the deliverable.
